extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, race, migration, and policing; researchers and advanced readers interested in post-war British urban history and social policy
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly chapter-level analysis of the structural relations among race, class, migration, housing and policing in post-war Britain, focusing on how policy and economy reproduce black labour's subordinate position and the social dynamics of 'colony' life and youth resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigration legislation as attack on citizenship rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigration legislation from the mid-1960s onwards must therefore be understood as an attack on the citizenship rights and status of black workers, as the precondition for a tighter regulation of the migrant labour supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes lowering/tightening of skill requirements, severe restriction on the entry of dependants, and transformation of status through patrial/non-patrial and Old/New Commonwealth distinctions; increased vouchers to 'proper aliens' (guest workers) from poorer European countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/status distinctions transforming settlers into 'guest workers'
rubrics_metrics.description: The patrial/non-patrial and Old/New Commonwealth distinctions transformed migrant labour from the status of settler to that of 'guest worker'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal reclassification reduces settlement rights and access to dependants, effectively subordinating earlier settler populations and facilitating a regulated temporary labour supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political restrictions and racist organisation as structural, not merely attitudinal
rubrics_metrics.description: The political restrictions on blacks, the growth of 'racist' and explicitly anti-immigrant organisations, and the toughening of social discipline in areas of black residence cannot therefore be attributed solely to 'discriminatory attitudes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are structural features arising from the incorporation of black labour into metropolitan capital and used during recession to recomposite black labour; they are not reducible to individual employer or personal prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migrant labour as the most exploited sector and a disinflationary mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Migrant labour now provides the sector of labour subject to the highest rate of exploitation and is playing a critical role as a disinflationary factor in periods of capitalist recession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to monopoly capital tendencies and falling rates of profit; migrant labour is closely integrated with cyclical movements of expansion and recession in heavily capitalised production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residential concentration as a key structural feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The residential concentration of the black immigrant population in inner-city areas is one of the most significant features of their structural position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caused by relatively cheap housing, search for solidarity, gap between low black wages and rising housing costs elsewhere, discriminatory practices by agents and mortgage companies, absentee landlords' neglect, eviction and redevelopment pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing market processes producing homelessness and squatting among young black adults
rubrics_metrics.description: As black adults' situation worsened, single young men or women seeking to leave home found decent accommodation virtually impossible to obtain, leading to drifting, sleeping rough, homelessness and squatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher unemployment among young blacks means inability to pay rents; legislative and market changes (redevelopment, demolition) reduce availability of rented property relevant to black families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race as a structural constituent in reproduction of class relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Race is a structural feature of the position and reproduction of the black labour force — it helps reproduce class relations in a racially stratified and internally antagonistic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These race-specific mechanisms have differentiated impacts by sex and generation and underpin political fragmentation of the class into racially segmented fractions placed in competition with one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical imprint of imperialism on racial divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of commercial colonial exploitation and subsequent imperialism imprinted racial supremacy across English social life and established internal relations of opposition and competition within the British working class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperialism provided both economic benefits (exploitation of colonial economies, labour supplements) and ideological weapons (racist ideologies) used to divide and control the metropolitan working class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital reproducing an internally divided labour force via immigrant labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital continues to reproduce labour in an internally divided form by importing immigrant labour to fill jobs which the indigenous workforce will no longer do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process reproduces differential class interests between British and colonial working classes and sustains segmented labour markets under capitalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between assimilation, acceptance, and colony formation strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad strategies exist for black communities: assimilation (largely ruled out), acceptance (taking on subordinate second-class role and informal segregation), and construction of a 'colony' or enclave as a fuller extension of separateness and marginality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assimilation is impractical and unwelcome by white society; acceptance produces informal segregation; colony formation provides a material base for cultural cohesion and alternative survival strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colony/enclave as material base for cultural revival and survival
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal colonies provided the material base for a cultural revival: a visible 'West Indian consciousness' and regenerated 'black consciousness', and the development of native quarters, churches, clubs, sound systems and black-owned shops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colony life also enabled informal economies and semi-legal practices (hustling) that sustain both economic and cultural survival within the enclave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hustling as a survival strategy distinct from organised crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Hustling is a common, necessary and familiar survival strategy for 'colony' dwellers, different from professional crime: it takes place on the blind side of the law, involves moving terrains and ad hoc rackets, and sustains the colony's informal economy and social infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hustlers provide social connections, access to scarce goods and cultural services (clubs, parties); most hustlers do not succeed long-term and many suffer violent or degrading outcomes; hustling increases with black unemployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State/media narratives constructing 'respectable' vs 'undesirable' blacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Official and media discourses often differentiate 'respectable blacks' from an 'undesirable element', using crime and moral arguments to stigmatise parts of the black community and justify surveillance or deportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home Office memoranda and press headlines linked black colonies with vice and crime, prompting calls for tighter supervision and powers against 'undesirables'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police presence and surveillance as a key mechanism of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of the police into black neighbourhoods (e.g., post-1958 riots) established a presence from which they have never withdrawn, generating fears of police discrimination and sustained surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policing became embedded in the neighbourhood as a control force, contributing to the 'unsettling' and political mobilisation of black communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second generation born into the colony faces intensified closure of opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-generation black youth are born into the colony and experience racial segregation as a given; they are better educated but encounter a closed occupational and opportunity structure on grounds of race rather than competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They lack the first-generation's optimism about improvement; political mobilisation, legal restrictions and police harassment have often made conditions palpably worse for the younger generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race as the principal modality of consciousness and resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Race performs a double function: it is both a structural constituent of social order and the principal modality through which black members of the class experience, comprehend and resist their structured subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through racialised consciousness, black workers perceive their exploitation and organise resistance; race mediates both experience and political culture (e.g., black consciousness movements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural expropriation and school segregation shaping youth identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Black youth experience cultural expropriation through the school system and tend to segregate along ethnic lines in schools, seeing few signs of adult social integration between races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This educational and social segregation contributes to a distinctive black youth consciousness and reinforces perceptions that 'English society is racist — it works through race.'
